flashcards.a: (1) Decision requested w/ size, deadline, default-if-silent; (2) problem + why-now with dated forcing function; (3) 2-3 evidence numbers with sources; (4) cheapest-path proposal; (5) value band vs cost band; (6) alternatives INCLUDING do-nothing; (7) top-3 risks x mitigations; (8) kill condition. ~450-600 words.

flashcards.q: Why state 'silence = no' in an ask?
flashcards.a: It prevents zombie approvals that die later during execution when someone finally objects. Explicit defaults surface real blockers early while they're still fixable; ambiguity collects interest until it's expensive.

flashcards.q: How do you present numbers so finance doesn't shred them?
flashcards.a: Ranges not points; each tagged measured/modeled/assumed with provenance; sensitivity table showing conclusion survives pessimistic value x doubled costs (or saying plainly when not); weakest link named proactively; definitions aligned with finance's own metrics. Meta-rule: defend your worst number, not your best.

flashcards.q: Describe the pre-alignment sequence before any funding review.
flashcards.a: Map deciders/influencers/blockers -> socialize the PROBLEM statement first (cheaper to agree than solutions) -> preview draft with strongest skeptic asking 'what would kill this?' -> answer their objection IN the doc -> final sent >=48h ahead with comments open -> meeting covers unresolved issues only -> explicit decision/owner/date.

flashcards.q: Why structure big asks as tranches?
flashcards.a: Headcount/dollars face scrutiny proportional to size; three consecutive $105K evidence-gated decisions are routine where one $315K faith-based ask dies. Each tranche carries a re-up gate ('evidence >= X% of value-band midpoint'), giving deciders stop-loss optionality and you built-in feedback.

flashcards.q: What does Netflix's 'farming for dissent' change about meetings?
flashcards.a: Dissent is collected BEFORE meetings via circulated proposals naming objectors and addressing objections - converting ambushes into footnotes and skeptics into co-signers. Meetings ratify what writing already settled.

flashcards.q: What belongs in a full business case beyond the one-pager?
flashcards.a: Three-scenario sensitivity matrices, cohort-level assumptions, NPV/payback framing, dependency/sequencing plan, staffing plan, risk register with owners, compliance/security review status, decision timeline with re-up gates. The long version exists for finance/legal/security - reviewers who kill projects quietly in back-channels.

flashcards.q: Deferred with 'great doc, wrong quarter.' Response?
flashcards.a: Diagnose the no (capacity / priority / courtesy-deferral = slow no); ask 'what would need to be true for Q2?'; attach to blocker's success metric or shrink tranche into discretionary space; set dated follow-up on the stated condition; meanwhile ship the cheapest unblockable slice so next cycle arrives with data.

When it improves only PASSAGE rather than decision QUALITY: predetermined outcomes, objections suppressed via unrelated side-deals, identical talking points across 1:1s. Legitimate alignment improves assumptions and removes surprises while keeping the outcome genuinely open.

flashcards.q: How do you build reputation that makes future asks cheaper?
flashcards.a: Report actuals vs promised bands quarterly ESPECIALLY on misses; kill own failing projects publicly per pre-written conditions; share credit precisely; start with small reversible well-bounded asks. Reputation = historical hit-rate plus honesty-about-misses stored in others' memories.

flashcards.q: Writing for a 90-second exec read: mechanics?
flashcards.a: Ask + stakes inside first 50 words; one-screen self-sufficiency; assertion-style headings carrying conclusions; numbers in tables; kill hedging (hedges transfer doubt upward); methodology/caveats in linked appendices. Test: hand to an outsider for 90s - can they state ask/stakes/deadline?

flashcards.q: Peer torpedoes proposals in meetings despite friendly 1:1s. Playbook?
flashcards.a: Verify pattern via minutes; write their objections down seriously (some are unprocessed factual disputes); circulate docs earlier with written-dissent deadlines; redirect in-meeting: 'addressed page two - which test does the mitigation fail?'; one private direct relationship conversation if it persists. Escalation only for genuine bad faith.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT write a document and just act?
flashcards.a: Reversible two-way-door calls inside your authority (flags, tooling trials) - act then document outcomes; emergencies invert the pipeline; early-trust phases need visible delivery before proposals land. Documents multiply existing credibility, don't substitute. Boundary test: state which door you're walking through BEFORE walking through it.
